# Lithium

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pharmacology > Neurologic and psychiatric > Lithium*

[Original Article Link](/library/zN0rdg)

---

## Summary

Lithium is a psychiatric medication used primarily as a first-line therapy for <u>bipolar disorder</u>. It is also used in treatment-resistant <u>depression</u> to augment <u>antidepressants</u>. The specific mechanism by which lithium acts to stabilize mood is not definitively known, but it is thought to be due to inhibition of the phosphoinositol cascade. Common side effects include gastrointestinal <u>distress</u> (<u>nausea</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>), <u>polyuria</u>, <u>polydipsia</u>, and <u>tremor</u>. Lithium therapy has a very <u>narrow therapeutic index</u>; frequent monitoring is therefore required to prevent toxicity.

---

## Pharmacodynamics

* Mechanism of action: While the mechanism of action has not been definitively established, inhibition of the phosphoinositol cascade is thought to result in mood stabilization.

* <u>Steady state</u>: usually reached 4–5 days after initiation or a change in dosage

---

## Pharmacokinetics

* 95% of lithium is excreted by the <u>kidneys</u>.

* It is freely filtered at the <u>glomerulus</u> and mostly reabsorbed in the <u>proximal convoluted tubule</u> via <u>sodium</u> channels. [[1]](/library/0vbeAv)

---

## Indications

* First-line therapy for <u>bipolar disorder</u>

* Mood stabilization in patients with acute <u>mania</u>

* <u>Maintenance therapy</u>

* Augmentation in treatment-resistant <u>depression</u>

---

## Adverse effects

### Overview [[2]](/library/pEbL9v)




Adverse effects occur at therapeutic levels (0.4–1.0 mEq/L) but tend to be more severe at peak serum concentration of the drug.




#### Nonspecific




* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>

* Weight gain

* Dry oral <u>mucosa</u>

* <u>Leukocytosis</u>





#### Motor




* Fine <u>tremor</u> 

* Nonprogessive, symmetric, fine <u>postural tremor</u> in the <u>distal</u> ends of upper extremities

* Typically occurs when lithium therapy is started or the dose is increased but can occur at any time during the course of treatment

* Often decreases spontaneously over time

* <u>Muscle weakness</u>





#### <u>Dermal</u>




* <u>Acne</u>

* Worsening <u>psoriasis</u>

* <u>Hair</u> thinning





#### Cardiac [[3]](/library/tmYXhp)




* <u>ECG</u> changes: <u>T-wave</u> depressions (most common), <u>U waves</u>, <u>repolarization</u> abnormalities

* <u>Sinus node dysfunction</u> (most commonly <u>sinus bradycardia</u>)





#### <u>Thyroid</u>




* <u>Hypothyroidism</u> (often subclinical) 

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u> should be performed every 6–12 months during ongoing treatment

* Lithium-induced <u>hypothyroidism</u>, should be treated with replacement therapy (<u>levothyroxine</u>).

* There is usually no need to discontinue lithium therapy.

* Lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism

* Caused by the elevation of the <u>calcium</u>-sensing setpoint of the <u>parathyroid glands</u> and induction of <u>parathyroid hormone</u> production

* Leads to <u>hypercalcemia</u>

* <u>Goiter</u> (particularly in second and <u>third trimester</u> of <u>pregnancy</u>)





#### Renal




* <u>Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus</u>

* Pathophysiology: lithium interferes with <u>ADH</u> signaling → ↓ <u>aquaporins</u> (water channels) on the <u>collecting duct</u> cell's surface → ↓ water molecules are reabsorbed and <u>kidneys</u> are unable to concentrate urine → ↑ free water excretion

* Clinical features: <u>polyuria</u>, <u>nocturia</u>, and <u>polydipsia</u> → ↑ risk of <u>dehydration</u> and subsequent <u>lithium toxicity</u>

* <u>Chronic interstitial nephritis</u> (lithium-associated nephropathy) 

* <u>Interstitial</u> <u>fibrosis</u>, focal <u>nephron</u> <u>atrophy</u>, tubular cysts with chronic use

* Risk correlates with the cumulative dose and duration of lithium use.

* Often occurs in the setting of <u>nephrogenic DI</u>

* Can progress to <u>chronic kidney disease</u>





> [!NOTE]
> LITHIUM: “Lithium can cause Irregular Thyroxine levels (<u>hypothyroidism</u> or <u>hyperthyroidism</u>), Heart (<u>Ebstein anomaly</u>), nephrogenic <u>diabetes</u> Insipidus, and Uncontrolled Muscle movements (<u>tremor</u>).”




### Treatment of adverse effects [[4]](/library/Qwaui5)[[5]](/library/HmYKSp)




* General measures

* Reassurance, avoidance of exacerbating factors (e.g., <u>caffeine</u>, <u>stress</u>), and follow-up

* Dosage adjustment

* Use of short-acting lithium preparations, divided doses, or a different lithium salt (e.g., <u>citrate</u> instead of carbonate)

* Reducing the total daily dose of lithium if serum lithium concentration is close to the upper limit of the therapeutic range

* <u>Tremor</u>: <u>beta blockers</u> (e.g., <u>propranolol</u>) if persistent or severe <u>tremor</u>

* <u>Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus</u>: <u>amiloride</u>  [[6]](/library/Esa89N)





### <u>Lithium poisoning</u>




* Toxic effects occur at serum levels > 1.5 mEq/L. [[7]](/library/ZKWZUm0)

* For details and management, see “<u>Lithium poisoning</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Monitoring serum levels of lithium is important because of its narrow therapeutic window.




We list the most important adverse effects. The selection is not exhaustive.

## Contraindications

* <u>Absolute contraindications</u> [[8]](/library/tsaX9N)[[9]](/library/WoYPaJ) 

* Advanced <u>renal failure</u> (<u>creatinine clearance</u> < 30 mL/min)

* Severe cardiovascular disease

* <u>Relative contraindications</u>

* Concurrent <u>diuretic</u> use

* <u>Dehydration</u>, <u>sodium</u> depletion

* Desired <u>pregnancy</u>/<u>pregnancy</u>: lithium can freely cross the <u>placental barrier</u>, inevitably resulting in fetal lithium exposure

* ↑ Risk of <u>miscarriage</u>  and neonatal complications (e.g., longer duration of hospital stays, higher rate of <u>CNS</u> and neuromuscular complications) [[10]](/library/5Y1ip20)[[11]](/library/MY1Mp20)

* <u>Teratogenicity</u>;  (especially in the <u>first trimester</u>): ↑ risk of cardiovascular <u>malformations</u> (in particular <u>Ebstein anomaly</u>)

* If lithium is needed during <u>pregnancy</u>, aim for the minimum effective dose and monitor serum levels regularly.

* <u>LARCs</u> are generally the preferred method of <u>contraception</u> because they are easy to use and have low failure rates. [[12]](/library/LY1wp20)





> [!TIP]
> Alternative <u>maintenance treatment</u> options for <u>bipolar disorder</u> include <u>lamotrigine</u>, <u>valproate</u>, and <u>carbamazepine</u>. <u>Valproate</u> and <u>antipsychotics</u> (e.g., <u>olanzapine</u>, <u>quetiapine</u>) can be used for treatment of acute <u>mania</u> and <u>hypomania</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Before prescribing lithium to women of child-bearing age, evaluate <u>thyroid</u> function, renal function, and <u>human chorionic gonadotropin</u> levels to rule out <u>pregnancy</u>.




We list the most important contraindications. The selection is not exhaustive.
